item.title: MeerKAT directly detects faint hydrogen signal from the distant universe
item.description: Astronomers from the University of Manchester and the University of the Western Cape have directly detected an extremely faint radio signal from hydrogen gas billions of light-years away, opening a powerful new way to map the large-scale structure of the universe. Using South Africa's MeerKAT radio telescope, the international team measured radio emissions from neutral hydrogen dating back to a time when the universe was several billion years younger than it is today. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Remote work offers flexibility, but at the cost of learning opportunities for young workers
item.description: Six years after the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the shift to remote work, hybrid and remote arrangements have become an established part of the labor market. About one in five Canadians now works remotely some or all of the time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Diatom sequencing project finds striking genetic differences among microscopic algae
item.description: An international team of more than 100 scientists has taken a major step toward unlocking the secrets of some of Earth's tiniest but most important organisms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New AI approaches to help understand complex biological data
item.description: Researchers at Cardiff University have presented two studies at the 2026 International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026) that address fundamental challenges in modern AI: understanding the complex geometry and relationships within data and recognizing patterns that occur across very different scales. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New AI model maps the ion binding sites that control how proteins work
item.description: Researchers at Constructor University and Constructor Labs have developed BiteNetI, a deep-learning model that locates the binding sites of 14 biologically important ion types directly in three-dimensional protein structures. The model needs only several seconds per structure and reaches two- to threefold higher accuracy than most existing predictors, including Google DeepMind's AlphaFold 3. The study, authored by Igor Kozlovskii and Petr Popov, has been published in the journal Communications Biology. The tool provides an open-access platform that could help accelerate drug discovery and the… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Historic Engines Take Their Place on Artemis III
item.description: On Aug. 24, technicians at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began installing the four RS‑25 engines in the core stage of the agency’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket that will carry the Artemis III crew into low Earth orbit in 2027. Each RS‑25 engine has a unique serial number that records its detailed flight […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gary Daines

item.title: AI tool detects unusual satellite behavior to improve space safety
item.description: A new AI model can monitor satellites and spot anomalies in their behavior, reducing the risk of in-orbit collisions, according to new research published in the journal Expert Systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ten-channel photonic interface links neutral-atom qubits in parallel
item.description: A research group in Japan has demonstrated a world-record 10-channel multiplexed quantum photonic interface based on an integrated waveguide array, a key technology for optically interconnecting multiple quantum computers. The study is published in the journal Optica. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 9/11 responders passed effects of trauma to their children, study finds
item.description: Although it's been 25 years since the World Trade Center collapsed after terrorists flew commercial airplanes into each of the center's two towers, the trauma experienced by many first responders and recovery workers is still being felt by their children. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Non-police safety practitioners reduce crime
item.description: Non-police community guardians can effectively reduce crime by building relationships in urban disorder hotspots, according to a study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Geomagnetic superstorm shook GPS accuracy across the US—its timing may have averted agricultural losses
item.description: On Nov. 11, 2025, Earth experienced a severe geomagnetic storm triggered by solar flares and coronal mass ejections from an active sunspot region. While this kind of storm brings beautiful auroras admired in many areas around the world, it can also cause ionospheric disturbances that disrupt radio waves and affect crucial technologies. A new study, published in Geophysical Research Letters, found that disruptions caused by this storm scrambled GPS signals in areas where such disruptions have never been reported. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Largest review finds formal ethics education improves students' moral reasoning
item.description: How important is it that kids learn to tell right from wrong? Businessman and former university chancellor David Gonski recently called for ethics classes to be rolled out in all Australian schools to boost social cohesion. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anti-influenza therapies that target the host
item.description: A drug that targets the host rather than the virus could get around the problem of antiviral resistance. Every year, hundreds of thousands of people die of seasonal influenza caused by infection with influenza A and B viruses. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Experiment sees surprising result in search for dark matter
item.description: For the better part of a century, people have been trying to understand dark matter. This invisible substance makes up roughly 85% of the mass in the universe but has never been directly detected. Determining exactly what it is remains one of the biggest questions about our world. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: For a century, journalists have had a voluntary ethics code. Editors are giving it an AI-era reboot
item.description: Walk into a corner of a newsroom somewhere and you can often find it affixed to a bulletin board, perhaps peeking out from behind the coffee pot: the Society of Professional Journalists's Code of Ethics. It's less than a thousand words, fitting neatly on a poster. Publicado también por: The Independent - World. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ice island survives run-in with Joe Island
item.description: Summer is prime iceberg season in Greenland's glacier-fed fjords, and 2026 was no exception. Especially notable was the berg that broke from Petermann Glacier along Greenland's northwest coast in August. Roughly the size of St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands, it was the largest calving event by any Arctic glacier since 2020. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Warming winters weaken New Hampshire forest's carbon sink over 20 years
item.description: Can we count on forests to continue absorbing the carbon dioxide that's warming our world? A new study from researchers at NAU and the University of New Hampshire says ... maybe not. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Peacemaker program linked to 61% decline in gun violence deaths and injuries
item.description: A new study by researchers at UC Berkeley's Center for Global Healthy Cities, published in JAMA Network Open, found that the California city of Richmond's Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in the city's firearm homicides and injury shootings over the past 14 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Marmite lures discovery from lake depths
item.description: Dr. Roe Stuart didn't find a taniwha in the unexplored depths of New Zealand's lakes—but they may have found a new species of fish. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ultrafast snapshots reveal the first moments on the way from light to electricity
item.description: Physicists at the University of Graz (Austria), in collaboration with colleagues from Marburg University and Forschungszentrum Jülich (Germany), have achieved a scientific breakthrough. For the first time, the generation of electrical energy from light has been filmed and described theoretically. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Screening tool amplifies tiny changes in protein levels within cells
item.description: Imagine a brain teaser where the challenge is to spot the difference between two nearly identical sandcastles. The only difference? The removal of three grains of sand. Scientists face a similarly exasperating challenge when looking at changes in protein levels within our cells, where small fluctuations can mean the difference between health and disease or a drug working and not working. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ecological collapse in the world's largest mangrove forest is a preview of what's to come
item.description: The first thing that struck us wasn't the missing trees, but the missing water. In May 2026, we visited the Sundarbans, a mangrove forest in the delta where the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers meet in the Bay of Bengal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: It turns out that Orion's much-maligned heat shield performed really well
item.description: Independent safety officials also have high praise for changes by NASA leadership. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: Q&A: Can you trust online ratings in the age of 'review bombing'?
item.description: Before buying a product, booking a hotel or streaming a movie, many people check online reviews. But not every glowing recommendation or one-star takedown reflects a genuine customer experience. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Resin-mounted wallaby teeth reveal rare 1,200-year-old ornaments in Queensland
item.description: While sorting through animal bones in a rock shelter in Queensland, Australia, archaeologists came across a tooth where something was "not quite right." Stuck to the tip of its root was a blackish-brown ball of glue-like resin. Eleven more teeth with the same sticky substance were found, making them the only known instance of this type of tooth ornament found outside burials in northeastern Australia and the first in the Cape York Peninsula (CYP), the new study published in Australian Archaeology reports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Three common study myths busted by a learning expert—and better strategies to use instead
item.description: As high school and university students approach exam periods, study sessions often increase in frequency and intensity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trump’s North Korea hope, US revokes visas, China’s rocket force: 7 global relations reads
item.description: We have selected seven of the most interesting and important news stories covering global relations from the past few weeks. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Trump says he plans to meet Kim Jong-un this year, citing good relationship US President Donald Trump said that he planned to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un later this year, despite Pyongyang denying that the two leaders were in direct communication. Read the full story here. 2. China... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: SCMP

item.title: Old-growth tropical forests bear lasting legacy of ancient Maya civilization
item.description: Rainforests in Central America that have remained largely untouched by modern human activities could bear the invisible imprint of ancient Maya civilizations. New research has found that forest structure in Belize, such as canopy height and leaf density, may be influenced by how the Maya transformed and used the land thousands of years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fieldwork safety emerges as a structural challenge for ecological research
item.description: A new Viewpoint in the journal BioScience argues that gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV) in ecological fieldwork should be understood not as a series of isolated incidents but as a structural problem rooted in how field research is organized, with broad consequences for the knowledge such research produces. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 324-million-year-old fossil reveals an insect that lived between land and water
item.description: Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Primary school food provision 'complex, fragmented and lacking central oversight', study reveals
item.description: A lack of central oversight and shifting catering models in primary schools could be putting children's dietary health at risk, according to new research led by the University of York. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Some of Australia's biggest companies are planning for an unbearable climate future
item.description: Even as unprecedented fires and heat waves rage across Europe, scientists track the retreat of Antarctic sea ice and a supercharged El Niño system heads our way, Australia's largest companies are forecasting business as usual in a much hotter world. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Growing bacteria line up single-file, then buckle in liquid crystals
item.description: When scientists study bacteria that are not in a Petri dish or a test tube but in environments that more closely mimic their actual microbial habitats, they often find delightfully unexpected behaviors. For Sujit Datta, a professor of chemical engineering, bioengineering and biophysics at Caltech, those oddities are an invitation to apply physics to exciting new puzzles. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Drone laser scans map more than 1,000 trees across 90-acre campus
item.description: It took one drone, 300 million laser data points and seven teams of students on foot to map Wake Forest University's trees. Led by Ovidiu Csillik, an assistant professor of remote sensing in the environment and sustainability studies program, the project produced a publicly accessible, interactive 3D digital map of more than 1,000 trees and helped the university earn international accreditation as a Level II arboretum. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Starship could create more debris than an anti-satellite test if it explodes in orbit
item.description: As Starship, the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, gears up for an attempt to finally reach Earth’s orbit, experts say the risk of an in-flight catastrophe – and a cloud of debris – “needs to be of concern”. Elon Musk’s SpaceX is expected to launch the Starship spacecraft and Super Heavy booster for the launch system’s 14th test flight and first orbital test flight later this month. According to one aerospace expert, if the Starship’s upper stage explodes in orbit it could produce debris... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Victoria Bela

item.title: Bees see the world in more ways than previously thought
item.description: The honey bee has held a special place in vision research. It is one of the best-studied insects, and much of what scientists know about how bees perceive the world is based on studies of honey bees. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mindfulness may lower blood pressure in just 8 weeks
item.description: Mindfulness, gratitude, and optimism training may improve blood pressure, inflammation, and other heart-health measures within just eight to 12 weeks. The strongest programs paired daily practice with regular reinforcement, suggesting that improving psychological well-being could become another tool for protecting cardiovascular health. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A supermassive black hole erupted in X-rays, and its radio jets followed 300 days later
item.description: By combining roughly two decades of observations from NASA's Swift X-ray Telescope with radio monitoring, astronomers have caught a supermassive black hole at the heart of the Perseus Cluster suddenly flaring in X-rays, and about 300 days later, its powerful radio emission flared too. Their paper describing the connection between this black hole's accretion disk and the jets it launches was submitted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 13 and accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Letters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover why snake embryos twist into spirals
item.description: Snake embryos begin life curled into a distinctive right-handed spiral, and scientists may finally know why. Their bodies grow faster than their guts, creating a tether that forces the lengthening embryo to buckle and twist inside the egg. Researchers reached the conclusion after studying more than 900 embryos and using CT scans to reveal the hidden anatomy behind the coils. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Research highlights hidden impact of domestic violence on women and their pets
item.description: New research from James Cook University has found that women experiencing domestic violence are often forced to choose between their own safety and the safety of their pets, with limited pet-inclusive crisis support contributing to additional trauma and distress. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reaching 90 without dementia doesn’t mean you’re in the clear
item.description: A study of people over 90 found that dementia risk remains strongly shaped by sex, race and genetics, with women and black participants facing notably higher risks. Intriguingly, some people stayed cognitively healthy despite carrying major risk factors, potentially offering clues to how the brain can resist dementia deep into old age. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: When exposed to air, new nanomaterial becomes magnetic at high temperatures
item.description: While fridge magnets are great for saving favorite recipes, modern magnetic materials are useful for improving fiber optics or quantum information science technology. On most fridge magnets the atoms are arranged in a repeated lattice structure called a "spinel." These structures are made up of three types of atoms, generically referred to as atoms "A," "B" and "X." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: UK researchers made a reef from 50 tonnes of coal waste; marine life arrived within 3 weeks
item.description: Researchers created an artificial reef from coal-fired power station waste in Poole Bay. Marine life began colonizing the structure almost immediately after its deployment. Adult lobsters and edible crabs reached the reef within three weeks of its placement. The structure attracted schools of pouting and supported reproduction for several species. This experiment showed industrial waste could become a productive marine habitat. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: How do you get middle schoolers to eat more fruit? Give them smoothies
item.description: At lunchtime in rural Maine middle schools, University of Maine researchers stood at two points in the cafeteria. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 12,000-year-old skeletons in Italy reveal a mother-daughter relationship
item.description: Archaeologists discovered two skeletons in an embrace within Romito Cave over twelve thousand years ago. Genetic analysis revealed these individuals were both female and closely related, likely mother and daughter. The younger skeleton showed a rare inherited disorder affecting growth and limb development. This finding confirms the existence of genetic diseases in ancient human populations. The discovery also suggests prehistoric communities provided care for individuals with physical limitations. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Engagement-driven curation can trap culture consumers in 'overfamiliarity,' leading to less long-term satisfaction
item.description: Sometimes you can be too good at your job. Take streaming services, like Spotify or Netflix. With engagement as their main goal, their recommendation algorithms typically identify the content a user engaged with most in the recent past and efficiently suggest more of the same. Content and genres that received limited engagement over a few weeks or months typically get dropped. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Without new landers or rovers, it's helicopters or bust for NASA's Mars program
item.description: NASA's cost estimate for SR-1 Freedom is $2.1 billion, but that doesn't include the helicopters. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clark

item.title: New research compares civil servant experiences under Trump in the US to those under Bolsonaro in Brazil
item.description: A new comparative survey of nearly 150 career civil servants (66 in the U.S. and 82 in Brazil) probed differences in bureaucratic responses to democratic backsliding among civil servants who served under U.S. President Trump and Brazilian President Bolsonaro. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A massive plume deep beneath Africa is pulling the continent apart
item.description: A vast plume rising from deep inside Earth may be responsible for mysterious movements along the East African Rift. The discovery reveals how forces deep in the mantle are working alongside shallower geological forces as the continent slowly pulls apart. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: In Japan's mountains, a different way to manage bears
item.description: As a sensor sounded, scientist Akiko Takii hurried to a bear trap deep in the forests of Nagano, Japan, where rising nationwide attacks have sparked fear and the culling of thousands of the animals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Samba’s fiery farewell recorded
item.description: Yesterday, on 31 August 2026, Samba reentered Earth’s atmosphere at 21:39:38 UTC / 23:39:38 CEST as the third of the four Cluster satellites. Samba had been lined up for a special 'targeted reentry' safely over the South Pacific Ocean, the precision so high that a plane could fly out from Tonga and successfully record its demise for reentry science. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Food innovation in your kitchen: Giving peas, beans and lentils a surprisingly meat-like bite
item.description: Separating things and then putting them back together is a common principle in industrial food production. Agricultural raw materials are broken down into their individual constituents, such as proteins, starches and fats, and the food industry then reassembles these building blocks into specific products. In many cases, not all of the harvested crop ends up in the food we eat. In some instances, byproducts are formed that must be reused outside the food industry. These processing steps can also lead to the loss of dietary fibers, vitamins and minerals in the finished product. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Declining star formation not caused by simple 'fuel crisis,' new measurements suggest
item.description: The universe has been having fewer and fewer stellar "babies." Over the past 4.5 billion years, the rate of star birth has crashed to less than half of what it once was. But here's the twist: the most essential "fuel" for making stars has barely decreased. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers catch sharks off NY's Hamptons, attach trackers to toothy predators
item.description: Just off one of New York's famed Hamptons beaches, shark researcher Greg Metzger reels in one of the day's prize catches: a young but powerful sand tiger shark. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Eruption of Sinabung volcano on Indonesia's Sumatra island prompts higher alert
item.description: Mount Sinabung on Indonesia erupted Monday, spewing a column of black ash and smoke 3,500 meters (11,482 feet) from the top of the mountain into the sky over Sumatra island. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Swift telescope is back, but time is running out
item.description: NASA has brought two of Swift’s telescopes back online after technical problems derailed a commercial mission intended to rescue the aging observatory by raising its orbit. With atmospheric drag pulling the spacecraft downward faster than expected, scientists may have only another month or two before Swift falls below a critical operating altitude. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: NASA delays Crew-13 launch after leak found on SpaceX Dragon
item.description: NASA and SpaceX have delayed Crew-13 after finding an oxidizer leak in the Dragon spacecraft’s propulsion system during prelaunch preparations. Engineers are investigating the problem before the four-person crew can begin its journey to the International Space Station. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Goodbye CPAP? New sleep apnea pill cuts breathing events by 44%
item.description: A once-nightly pill cut breathing interruptions by about 44% in a major phase 3 sleep apnea trial, while improving oxygen levels and disease severity. By strengthening the muscles that keep the airway open during sleep, AD109 could offer a new option for people unable to tolerate CPAP. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Chinese script evolved like a living organism driven by natural selection: study
item.description: Modern simplified Chinese characters form a tightly connected network from just 514 basic components that evolved through a process similar to natural selection, according to researchers who say their findings could change how Chinese writing is taught. “Chinese characters evolve like living organisms,” lecturer Xie Yonghui of Shanghai Normal University said on August 24. The research into the evolution of Chinese writing over thousands of years, led by Huang Wei, of Beijing Language and Culture... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Ice Island Survives Run-In With Joe Island
item.description: In summer 2026, a substantial iceberg calved from Petermann Glacier in northwest Greenland and swiftly drifted into Nares Strait, colliding with an island along the way. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists find a human-only gene that may help explain our brainpower
item.description: Scientists discovered that human microglia, immune cells that help shape developing brain circuits, can take four to eight years to mature instead of just weeks as they do in mice. The unusually slow process may help explain how the human brain develops its remarkable complexity and cognitive abilities. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Higher cutting could reduce annual bluegrass contamination in tall fescue seed
item.description: Harvesting tall fescue above annual bluegrass seed heads could help reduce contamination and seed-cleaning costs. Preliminary Oregon research found that cutting at 28 centimeters (11 inches) rather than 5 centimeters (2 inches) reduced annual bluegrass collected with the crop without consistently reducing tall fescue seed yield. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New hope in quest to solve mystery of MND hotspots
item.description: It is hoped new data from mandatory reporting of motor neurone disease (MND) cases will help researchers understand why there are hotspots in NSW, and what causes the disease. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Ceccato

item.title: High blood sugar may help cancer cells hide from the immune system
item.description: Researchers discovered a possible way cancer cells hide from the immune system: they build a thick, sugar-rich coating around themselves. High blood sugar can strengthen this protective shield under conditions that resemble the environment inside tumors, with the protein HSF1 playing a key role. Blocking this process could make cancer cells easier for the immune system to recognize and destroy. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: National survey measures full financial burden of community sport in Australia
item.description: The cost of playing community sports in Australia is far higher than previously understood, with a new national study led by Federation University finding families spend an average of $4,567 per child each year to keep their children playing sports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cover crops could ease the shift from perennial seed to annual crops
item.description: Transitioning an aging perennial forage seed stand into annual cropping can be difficult, particularly when the original crop persists or weeds establish after termination. Preliminary Canadian research suggests cover crops could help by suppressing regrowth and weeds, retaining biomass and cycling nutrients. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Drones take farming to new heights
item.description: High above the fields of the Morven Sustainability Lab, drones equipped with heat and light sensors are changing what it means to farm smarter. This month, researchers and students from the University of Virginia, NASA and the University at Buffalo tested drone technology by flying more than 100 feet (30 meters) above crops to measure plant health at UVA's 2,900-acre (1,170-hectare) research facility. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nasa scientists grew corn in space and found that microgravity changed root and shoot growth
item.description: NASA's recent experiments indicate that corn seeds struggle with directional growth in microgravity environments. Without Earth's gravitational cues, the roots and shoots exhibit erratic growth patterns. Similarly, other plants like Arabidopsis thaliana face similar challenges in space. To prepare for longer missions, NASA is actively designing systems to counterbalance the absence of gravity, underscoring the importance of understanding plant behavior for future food cultivation in space. item.title: Important role of plastid ion channels in plant stress response identified
item.description: When plants are attacked by herbivores or pathogens, they must respond rapidly while also preparing for potential future attacks. Calcium, a cellular second messenger, and the plant hormone jasmonic acid play important roles in this response. Within seconds of an injury, the plant generates calcium waves that relay information about the attack. At the same time, the synthesis of jasmonic acid is initiated in the chloroplast, triggering, through several intermediate steps, the expression of defense genes in the cell nucleus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sliding sugars offer simpler, smarter route to precision liver-targeted therapies
item.description: Targeted drug delivery directly to the liver has unlocked major breakthroughs across medicine, but constructing the chemical key to enter liver cells remains complex and costly. Today, researchers at Kumamoto University, in collaboration with the National University of Singapore, have unveiled a nature-inspired solution that bypasses synthetic bottlenecks by giving single sugar molecules room to move. Their findings are published in the journal Advanced Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Even ancient bacteria possessed intercellular communication structures like humans today, study finds
item.description: Communication between cells in plants, animals and humans takes place via specialized connecting structures. An international team led by biologists from Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU) and involving the University of Tübingen has now discovered that the regulation of very similar structures was already present in multicellular bacteria, implying that it must have originated much earlier in the course of evolution. In their paper published in The EMBO Journal, the researchers describe how the exchange of calcium plays a central role in bacteria, just as it does in humans. Fuente: Phys.org.
